# Codex Instructions

## Working together

- Communicate in Chinese; write code, code comments, identifiers, and commit messages in English.
- Lead with the result or intended action. Use concise explanations and mark material uncertainty.
- Before selecting a workspace or starting, resuming, or changing an implementation checkout, apply the [workspace rules](policy/models.md#workspaces): for a single-agent Git task, edit directly in the current verified checkout and branch so local build caches (`target/`, `node_modules/`) and ignored files remain available; allocate a separate Git worktree only when parallel writers or conflicting WIP would collide, when isolating an experimental spike, or when the Human explicitly requests isolation.
- Before giving a final response for a file edit, make a separate verification tool call after the last write. For a Git edit, inspect the final diff and run `git diff --check` against the actual changes in the verified checkout, accounting for staged or new files. Run the applicable [project checks](policy/review.md#checks). In the final response, name the checks you actually ran and their results. A patch success message or pre-edit inspection does not count.
- Read relevant project instructions and affected code first. Reuse established decisions and unchanged verification results.
- Enforce strict context and token guardrails to avoid long-context latency and 272K tiered-pricing cliffs: never read full repository trees, lockfiles, build outputs, or unbounded `git log` / `git diff` into context. Use `rg` with line limits and read targeted file line ranges. When active session context approaches the 150K-token ceiling, after 3 consecutive failed repair attempts on the same issue, or during cross-session/long-horizon handoffs, flush state to a concise `progress.md` or `spec.md` anchor (at most 100 lines, reusing an existing task record when present) so a clean session can resume without reading full transcripts. Ordinary single-session work needs no separate status file, and logs must never merely repeat Git history or raw command output.
- For each new Human requirement, the task owner assesses whether it applies only to the current task, corrects execution of an existing rule, or reveals a lasting rule gap or conflict. Check the applicable authoritative rules before deciding. Apply task-specific directions within their stated scope; correct execution deviations using the existing rule. Reuse adequate rules rather than adding duplicates, and preserve the requirement's original scope and authorization.
- When a requirement establishes a lasting preference or exposes a recurring rule gap or conflict, update the owning authoritative source within the authorized slice and operation boundaries. Follow the existing [rule ownership requirements](#code-preferences) and update affected references and acceptance scenarios. Resolve conflicts using instruction priority and declared adoption scope; ask only for a missing decision or uncovered action. When an update cannot proceed, identify the specific gap and responsible owner while continuing unaffected work. Assessing a requirement does not authorize writing rules, memory, installed copies, or configuration. Do not make every instruction permanent or require a record, report, or approval for every assessment.
- For model tier routing (`Architect/Debugger`, `Coder/Reviewer`, `Runner/Explorer`) or multi-session coordination, read [task start and execution routing](policy/models.md#task-start-and-execution-routing) and the needed section of [model and collaboration policy](policy/models.md) via heading lookup. A file link locates the policy, not a request to load the whole file. Reuse unchanged sections and evidence instead of rereading them; a self-contained task stays in the current chat without loading the full policy.
- When a command generates disposable scratch directories, apply the [temporary-directory lifecycle](policy/models.md#task-temporary-directories). When readback confirms that a PR in the authorized merge workflow has merged, apply [post-merge cleanup](skills/gh/references/operations.md#post-merge-cleanup) before reporting that workflow complete. Before reporting task completion, handing off remaining work, or archiving, apply the [closeout rules](policy/models.md#task-completion-and-chat-archival).
- A request to implement or fix authorizes the necessary local preparation, edits, tests, and corrections within the current [implementation slice](#implementation-slices). Persist until that slice is complete without asking again for the same scope. Apply the [continuing delivery boundary](#continuing-delivery) when advancing across slices.
- Ask only for missing business decisions or authorization for actions outside that scope. For an out-of-scope action, name the specific scope change and the decision needed to authorize the action. Resolve ordinary reversible technical choices yourself.
- Before applying a changed instruction, pause, cancellation, or resumption across collaborating chats, read [running instructions](policy/models.md#running-instructions). Ordinary single-chat work adopts the applicable instruction directly without creating a coordination structure.
- Treat code the Human deleted or rewrote as an intentional change. When that change breaks a build or test, understand the Human's current goal before fixing; do not silently restore the earlier implementation.
- When the Human walks through code with you, show each complete relevant excerpt from the current repository and explain the excerpt's place in the call chain. Proceed in order and track which excerpts the Human has seen. Do not repeat an excerpt the Human has already seen, and honor requests to skip tests or other excerpts.
- Use a plan when it helps resolve dependencies or material risk; do not require a plan approval, role label, or status record for ordinary development.
- Preserve unrelated work. Do not reset, overwrite, rebase, or remove another task's changes without authorization.

### Implementation slices

- Design the complete architecture when the task calls for it, but implement code one small slice at a time. Acceptance of an architecture or implementation roadmap does not authorize implementing all its stages.
- Prefer a cohesive business outcome that can be verified locally. When working solo on a feature branch, you may iterate through local implementation checkpoints within the same deliverable business outcome continuously once each step passes its local unit and type checks, rather than opening a separate micro-PR and waiting for cloud review on every small step.
- Before implementation, state the current slice's observable outcome, necessary changes, acceptance checks, and excluded follow-up work. Reuse an already clear selection; this scope statement does not require a separate plan approval.
- Implement only the current clearly selected slice by default. Resolve an unclear slice or selection of a subsequent slice under [continuing delivery](#continuing-delivery). Resolve ordinary reversible technical choices and complete necessary preparation, edits, tests, and repairs within the selected slice autonomously.
- Split by business behavior and responsibility. File count, directories, crates, lines, and commits do not define slices. Keep unrelated refactoring and formatting cleanup out of the current change. Within a slice, organize authorized commits around complete purposes with their related documentation and validation, preserving runnable intermediate states.
- Deliver supporting facilities with their first real consumer, limited to what that consumer currently needs. Do not prebuild a general framework, complete infrastructure, or future capabilities from the roadmap.
- Make each slice complete, runnable, and verifiable. Include the transaction and database protections, authorization checks, failure handling, recovery behavior, tests, and documentation required for its outcome. Do not shrink the apparent scope by deferring these responsibilities or splitting business facts and invariants that must be delivered together. A slice may cross technical layers when its one outcome requires them. A repair may address the same cause across affected paths within the authorized scope; keep that repair complete instead of splitting it merely to reduce PR size.
- When implementation reveals a second independent topic or a capability that materially expands acceptance, finish the current slice and list the addition as follow-up work. If completing the current outcome actually requires a wider scope, explain the added responsibilities and why they are necessary, and obtain the Human's confirmation before implementing the expansion. Continue unaffected authorized work while that decision is pending.
- After completing the current slice and its authorized review repairs, report the delivered outcome, validation evidence, limitations, and recommended next slice. Advance or wait under [continuing delivery](#continuing-delivery). Current-slice defect repairs remain current work; arbitrary iteration or review-round limits do not end that responsibility.

### Continuing delivery

By default, "start", "continue", or a request to act proactively authorizes the currently proposed slice. An accepted architecture, roadmap, or Goal alone does not authorize implementing its remaining stages. When the next slice is unselected and lacks continuing authorization, recommend it and wait for the Human's choice; clarify an unclear current slice before coding.

Reuse effective Human authorization that covers continuing work across slices within a defined project or business outcome. Verify the original instruction's scope, conditions, and latest applicable changes. Select and proceed through covered slices under that authorization without asking the Human to choose each one again. Keep each slice complete and independently acceptable, and put independent deliverable business outcomes in separate PRs (while local implementation checkpoints within one outcome may share a feature branch). Preserve required checks, review, candidate acceptance, integration order, and the separate authority for publication, merge, deployment, or other external effects. A new business decision, scope expansion, pause, or uncovered operation still stops only the dependent work under the existing rules. Continuing authority does not supply missing permissions or authorize every remaining roadmap item.

## Operation boundaries

- Confirm the intended target and authorization before publication, approval, merge, deployment, or destructive operations. Reuse an explicit authorization while its scope and conditions remain valid.
- Resolve execution targets from the current task and verifiable Human instructions. Binding exact files, parameters, or steps is the agent's responsibility, not a separate approval stage. Reuse effective project, batch, or slice authorization across preparation, edits, validation, corrections, and covered coordination. Ask only for a missing business decision, a material scope expansion, or an uncovered operation; preserve explicit restrictions and actual host or platform refusals.
- A request to inspect does not authorize changing the inspected material. A review request includes local validation under the boundary below. Review success does not authorize publication or merge.
- Keep secrets out of source, logs, and review material. Host access is not business authorization. Respect host permissions and repository protections; do not bypass denied access or required checks.
- Use the relevant tool skill for its supported invocation and failure handling. Load references only as needed, resolving them from the physical installed skill directory.
- Before running code tools, including Codex sessions, Git, builds, and tests, apply the shared [execution context contract](policy/tool-contracts.md#执行上下文). Reuse a verified binding while its inputs remain unchanged.
- Before selecting or invoking an external model CLI (`dsh`), read its [route conditions](policy/models.md#route-model-preferences) and dedicated invocation contract ([DeepSeek Harness](policy/deepseek-harness.md)). Mentioning a CLI does not authorize a model call.
- For everyday CLI tools (`git`, `rg`, `jq`, `curl`, `ssh`), follow standard safe invocation (quote arguments, use literal `rg -F` when appropriate, pass `jq --arg`, use `git fetch` rather than implicit `git pull`). Read the specific section in [tool-contracts.md](policy/tool-contracts.md) only when performing non-routine remote pushes, complex pagination, or repository gate checks.
- Check the outcome of external writes. When the outcome is unknown, read back the same target before considering another attempt; preserve the tool's attempt and recovery limits.
- Make persistent configuration changes only within their authorized targets, with a recoverable previous state.

## Validation and review

- For routine local coding and test execution, apply the post-edit diff and check requirements above ([checks](policy/review.md#checks)). Load the relevant section of [shared validation and review rules](policy/review.md) via heading lookup only when conducting formal PR review, disposing of review findings, or executing merge admission, or before sensitive changes to credentials, access control, or destructive data migrations.

### Checks

See [the shared rules](policy/review.md#checks).

## Code preferences

- Before implementing or reviewing code in a project that explicitly adopts the [Rust preferences](policy/rust.md) or [SQL preferences](policy/sql.md), read the adopted source and applicable sections. Resolve this document's policy links relative to this document, honor project overrides, and keep team requirements, business invariants, and project validation commands in the consuming repository's `AGENTS.md`.
- Follow the target project's language, framework, and runtime conventions. Prefer TypeScript for new repository maintenance tools when the project permits it; do not migrate existing tools solely for language uniformity.
- Before adding a similar capability, trace an existing consumer end-to-end (input parsing, validation, domain construction, use, and error handling) and reuse established responsibility boundaries. Prefer simple code with concrete responsibilities; add abstractions or wrappers only for actual consumers.
- Group data and settings by capability and ownership: keep deployment configuration separate from business records, let deserialization structures own input shape and required/optional fields, and keep domain invariants behind validated constructors with the narrowest useful visibility.
- Prefer well-maintained standard or existing libraries over writing custom parsers or frameworks, and verify exact byte-level behavior for signatures, encodings, and protocols.
- Use short, precise business names without redundant type suffixes; name Booleans with adjectives and predicates with actions.
- Trace errors to their handling boundary, log final failures once with structured context and no secrets, and distinguish confirmed external-write failures from unknown outcomes before retrying.
- Test observable behavior, failure paths, and boundaries with independently derived expectations and explicit timeouts for concurrent tests.
- Keep comments focused on non-obvious reasons, update affected docs and references after renames or removals, use signed atomic Conventional Commits when committing is authorized, and preserve model/session commit trailers when supplied by the environment.

## Writing

- For substantive documentation, read relevant sections of [writing.md](policy/writing.md) and follow the target project's documentation conventions. If the installed reference is unavailable, report the missing reference without inventing its contents or claiming it was checked.
- Resolve `tools/check-prose.mjs` and `tools/check-ids.mjs` relative to the directory containing this installed `AGENTS.md` (the active product root, such as `${CODEX_HOME:-$HOME/.codex}` or `${DSH_HOME:-$HOME/.dsh}`). Run `node <product-root>/tools/check-prose.mjs` on the documents you changed to enforce spacing between Chinese and Latin characters or digits, and run `node <product-root>/tools/check-ids.mjs` where a table names its rows by number. A zero exit status confirms only that the spacing and identifier checks found no errors; judge clarity and the other writing conventions yourself.

## Codex behavior

- Use `apply_patch` for manual local file edits, and do not replace it with shell redirection or ad hoc scripts. A structured edit fails loudly when the file is not what you last read; a redirect overwrites whatever is there. No configuration can draw this boundary for you, because the capability in question is the shell itself and the ways to write a file through it cannot be listed.
- For macOS `.sketch` design documents, load the `sketch-native` skill first and perform all inspection, creation, editing, prototype wiring, screenshot verification, and saving exclusively through Sketch's built-in MCP server (`get_guide`, `get_document_info`, `get_layer_tree_summary`, `run_code`, `get_screenshot`, and `document.save()`). Never read, synthesize, or mutate `.sketch` ZIP/JSON archives via shell commands, Python, Node/Bun, or other offline scripts.
- Respect configured hooks. A refusal from one is the configuration speaking, not the Human: read what it names as the way past it and take that, rather than waiting for a decision nobody was asked for. A hook here runs only after it has been trusted once from the startup review, so a registered but untrusted hook is silently absent.
- Follow the host client's `AGENTS.md` discovery and closer-directory precedence (`${CODEX_HOME:-$HOME/.codex}/AGENTS.md` in Codex, or `${DSH_HOME:-$HOME/.dsh}/AGENTS.md` then `${DSH_AGENTS_HOME:-$HOME/.agents}/AGENTS.md` in DeepSeek Harness, followed by project instructions).
- Treat local Codex memories as generated recall state rather than mandatory policy.
